1.pericope_label: In those days was Hezekiah sick unto death. And Isaiah the prophet the son of Amoz came unto him, and said unto him, Thus saith the LORD, Set thine house in order: for thou shalt die, and not live
debates: Whether the sickness fell before or after the Assyrian army was destroyed
Why he turned his face to the wall
Whether the prayer is self-satisfied or self-fortifying
outliers: Ellicott dates the illness before the destruction of the army, since the deliverance of the city is still future a few verses later, and rejects both the plague theory and the spoil theory that depend on the later date
Ellicott reads the sentence of death as a striking illustration of the conditional character of prophecy
Clarke explains the turning to the wall from the eastern custom of seating the honoured guest in the corner, where the walls separate him from the company

Ellicott hears self-satisfaction in the prayer and grants that the tears were probably less egotistic than the words, while Calvin denies any pleading of merit and calls it self-fortifying against despair
themes: Struck in the midst of a triumph
Orders given to a house and to a heart
Everything removed that would lead the mind aside
Tears more prevailing than words

4.pericope_label: Then came the word of the LORD to Isaiah, saying, Go, and say to Hezekiah, Thus saith the LORD, the God of David thy father, I have heard thy prayer
debates: Whether God reversed a decree or completed a test
Whether the promise about the city dates the sickness
Whether the shorter clause about the city is defective
outliers: Calvin answers the charge of a change of purpose by holding that death was threatened but not decreed, the threat being the instrument of the trial
Calvin explains the honourable title given to God in the second message as pointing out the cause and origin of the grace in the covenant
Calvin answers the argument that the promise about the city would be superfluous after the defeat, since the invader might have mustered a fresh army
Ellicott holds that the danger implied here need not be the famous invasion, an earlier attack having perhaps caused a general alarm
themes: A sting left in the wound
Groans rising out of a gulf of sorrow
A plank seized in shipwreck
A clause abrupt without the parallel

7.pericope_label: And this shall be a sign unto thee from the LORD, that the LORD will do this thing that he hath spoken
debates: Whether the sun moved or only the shadow
What kind of instrument the dial was
Whether asking for a sign was a fault
outliers: Gill argues that the sun itself went back, since a change confined to one dial would never have drawn the notice and inquiry of other nations
Ellicott proposes an exceedingly circumscribed refraction, a prolonged afterglow reviving the brightness of the day for one watching the steps
Calvin distinguishes signs given unasked, which are the usual case, from the rare ones granted on request, and warns that the rare case is no example
Calvin dismisses the story that the day of the death of Ahaz was shortened and the hours restored here, as destitute of evidence and probability
themes: A choice offered and the harder chosen
An obelisk standing on a flight of steps
A wonder as curiously limited as one darkness
Twelve degrees and fifteen years

9.pericope_label: The writing of Hezekiah king of Judah, when he had been sick, and was recovered of his sickness
debates: Why a new song was composed when psalms were at hand
Whether the king or the prophet wrote it
Where the two closing verses of the chapter belong
outliers: Henry lists the writings proper after a sickness, a memorial of the affliction, a record of the thoughts had while ill, a thanksgiving and a sealed covenant

Henry turns the excellence of the writing against its author, since the later history says he rendered not again according to the benefit, and adds that thanksgiving is good but thanksliving is better
Calvin holds that the more eminent a man is the more he is bound to consider himself placed upon a theatre, and warns at once against the ambition that magnifies its own name
Clarke warns that the parallel book deserts us here and that the text is probably corrupt as well as concise
themes: Affections offered in a man own words
Impressions that should never have worn off
A public record left for posterity
A psalm echoing an older book of suffering

10.pericope_label: I said in the cutting off of my days, I shall go to the gates of the grave: I am deprived of the residue of my years
debates: What the opening phrase means
Whether the fear of seeing God no more is a defect of faith
Whether the shepherd tent implies a future state
outliers: Ellicott rejects the rendering in quiet of my days on a point of fact, since the complaint could not come in the quiet of his life but only after it had passed
Calvin answers the objection to publishing such complaints by holding that nothing is more advantageous than a picture of a man overwhelmed with grief painted to the life
Ellicott detects a tone of reverence in the impersonal form of the statement, since the sufferer will not name the author of his trouble
Calvin reconciles the two ascriptions of the death, to the man and to God, since we give the grounds and he is the judge who inflicts
themes: A city of the dead with gates for its power
A web rolled up before it was finished
Consolation suppressed but not lost
A thread a man cuts for himself

13.pericope_label: I reckoned till morning, that, as a lion, so will he break all my bones: from day even to night wilt thou make an end of me
debates: Whether the verb means reckoned, roared or quieted myself
Whether the eyes are weakened or lifted on high
Whether the closing clause asks for surety or for advocacy
outliers: Ellicott renders the opening as quieting oneself, and makes the pathos turn on a morning that brought a fresh access of suffering
Calvin defends the comparison of God to a lion, since no fierceness in a beast strikes the terror felt at the bare mention of his name
Calvin holds that inarticulate groaning is heard by God and is more powerful than plain words where the Spirit is present
Ellicott finds behind the request for surety the figure of Death as a creditor, so that the judge who is also the accuser is asked to go bail for the accused
themes: A line repeated by mistake in the copies
A man reckoned the creature of a day
Three birds and three notes of lamentation
Eyes nearly worn out and still looking upward

15.pericope_label: What shall I say? he hath both spoken unto me, and himself hath done it: I shall go softly all my years in the bitterness of my soul
debates: Whether the opening question is joy or continued complaint
Whether the years to come are bitter or calm
Whether peace was lost to bitterness or gained through it
outliers: Calvin reads the question as complaint still running, and holds that we never cease to complain until restrained by fear of the power of God
Ellicott renders the following clause as walking at ease upon the trouble of the soul, and says the received version wrongly suggests a lifelong bitterness
Clarke notes that the play on words here is a figure this prophet frequently admits, and that it perfectly clears up the great obscurity of the passage
Ellicott points out that the words rendered delivered it are absent from the Hebrew, leaving the phrase thou hast loved me out of the pit of corruption
themes: Words failing where the rescue was sudden
A favour engraven on remembrance after the man is dead
Bitterness that was bitter for the sake of peace
Love that is itself the deliverance

18.pericope_label: For the grave cannot praise thee, death can not celebrate thee: they that go down into the pit cannot hope for thy truth
debates: In what sense the dead cannot praise God
Whether all the living are meant
Where the two closing verses of the chapter belong
outliers: Calvin grants that the language is too exclusive, since believers after death proclaim the praises of God with the angels, and explains it from the state of a man who thinks himself shut out of life by his own sins
Ellicott observes that the son who succeeded was not born until after this illness, so that the king may then have been childless and the want of an heir added bitterness to his grief
Keil and Delitzsch hold that the text has fallen into confusion, the last two verses having been dropped by oversight from the earlier promise and added in the margin
Calvin rejects the weaker rendering that it belongs to the Lord to save, since the king praises the work in which the power was proved
themes: A shadow world without hallelujahs
Despair that is dumb whether living or dead
Children given on condition of teaching them
A man expecting death one day and praising the next

21.pericope_label: For Isaiah had said, Let them take a lump of figs, and lay it for a plaister upon the boil, and he shall recover
debates: Where these two verses belong
Whether the figs were a real remedy or a contrary sign
Why the question about the house of God is recorded last
outliers: Keil and Delitzsch refer the two verses back to the earlier promise, holding that they belong there and not at the close
Calvin reports the view that the plaster was applied precisely because it could not cure, on the analogy of the bow set in gathering clouds, and rejects it
Calvin holds that God does not need secondary means but uses them when he sees fit, so that a promise loses nothing by being accompanied with a medicine
Calvin ends by holding that life is prolonged for piety and kind offices and the public exercises of religion, not for ease
themes: A writing ended and a note appended
Juice gathered green and dried in the shade
A sign that seems to promise the opposite
Years asked for in order to be spent
